title: Search-R1 Deconstruction: How the COLM 2025 Paper Clearly Explains 'RL + Search Engine'
subtitle: Reading a seminal work on the agentic RL paradigm from the perspective of structural anatomy
markdown: > Deconstruction Target: Search-R1: Training LLMs to Reason and Leverage Search Engines with Reinforcement Learning, COLM 2025. The authors are from UIUC, UMass Amherst, and Google Cloud AI Research, with first author Bowen Jin. The open-source code has garnered over 5k stars on GitHub. This article does only one thing: analyze why the structure of this paper is good. All numbers come from the main text and appendices of the latest version of the paper on arXiv, which can be cross-referenced with the original tables for verification. ## I. Why It Is Worth Deconstructing In the direction of 'R1 series methods + tool calling', Search-R1 is one of the most cited paradigmatic works by subsequent studies. It addresses a very simple question: Can a model learn purely through reinforcement learning to autonomously decide when to search, what to search for, and how to use search results during the reasoning process, completely bypassing the fixed workflow of Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and the reliance on supervised fine-tuning data for tool calling? This combination of a 'simple question + clean answer' makes it an ideal sample for deconstructing methodological papers. ## II. Three Acts of the Main Text: The Standard Skeleton of a Method Paper | Chapter | Responsibility | Key Points for Deconstruction | | --- | --- | --- | | 1 Introduction | Establishing the Argument | Identifies two specific flaws in previous approaches: the fixed retrieval workflow of RAG and the reliance on large-scale annotated data for tool-calling SFT | | 2 Related Works | Dual-Line Positioning | 2.1 LLMs and Retrieval, 2.2 LLMs and Reinforcement Learning; both lines are laid out to position the current work | | 3 Search-R1 | Main Methodology | Four subsections arranged in dependency order (expanded in the next section) | | 4 Main Results | Main Experiments | 7 QA datasets × 8 baselines, with the EM metric consolidated in a single main table | | 5 Analysis | Analysis | Four independent questions, each of which stands alone | | 6 Conclusions | Conclusion | Within one page | The main text consists of only 6 sections; formula derivations, hyperparameters, and case studies are all moved to Appendices A through J. The core assets of a methods paper are the methods and main results, while verification content is deferred. This trade-off is reflected very consciously in the section proportions. ## III. Layout of the Methods Section: Each Subsection Addresses a Necessary Condition for 'Making RL Work' The four subsections in Section 3 are worth examining one by one: | Subsection | Content | Necessary Condition Addressed | | --- | --- | --- | | 3.1 RL with a Search Engine | Unified formalization, including Loss Masking for Retrieved Tokens, and two variants: PPO and GRPO | Training objective established: Retrieved tokens do not enter the policy gradient | | 3.2 Multi-turn Calling | Rollout pseudocode for multi-turn search interactions (Algorithm 1) | Interaction flow established: A single rollout allows multiple searches | | 3.3 Training Template | Four-label template: think / search / information / answer | Interface established: How the model 'articulates' a search | | 3.4 Reward Modeling | Pure outcome-based rule-based EM reward | Signal established: 1 for correct answer, 0 for incorrect answer, no format-based reward | This order reflects a dependency sequence. The greatest engineering risk (retrieved tokens mixing into the policy gradient, causing training instability) is addressed in the first subsection using loss masking. After reading in order, the reader possesses all the elements necessary for reproduction. The "proposal and validation" closed loop of loss masking is also well-structured: the mechanism is proposed in Section 3.1, and its effects are validated in Section 5.4 and Table 4. For Qwen2.5-7B, the average EM with masking is 0.431 versus 0.343 without masking; for 3B, it is 0.303 versus 0.262. The complete study is included in Appendix D. A mechanism forms a complete chain of evidence from motivation and design to ablation studies. ## IV. The Analysis Section is the Second Contribution Area The four questions in Section 5 each address open issues of concern to the community: 1. **PPO vs. GRPO** (5.1): GRPO converges faster, while PPO starts slowly due to reliance on critic pre-training; however, GRPO suffers from reward collapse during long-term training, whereas PPO remains stable throughout. Therefore, the paper defaults to PPO. Typical data: for the 7B base model, PPO averages 0.431 compared to GRPO's 0.350; for 3B, GRPO's 0.312 is slightly higher than PPO's 0.303, confirming comparable final performance. Following the explosion of GRPO sparked by DeepSeek-R1, this comparison table directly addresses the hottest controversy at the time. 2. **Base vs. Instruct** (5.2): Base models serve as better starting points for training. 3. **Response Length and Effective Search Dynamics** (5.3): During training, response length first decreases, then increases, and finally stabilizes, while the number of effective searches continues to increase. 4. **Loss Masking Ablation** (5.4): See the previous section. The main table of the methods paper demonstrates "effectiveness," while the analysis section demonstrates "transferability." The PPO/GRPO comparison in Table 3 contributes an additional set of empirical conclusions that others can directly cite, representing the pinnacle of the analysis section. ## V. Appendices A to J: Structuring Reproducibility | Appendix | Content | | --- | --- | | A | Complete derivation of RL formalization formulas | | B | Experimental setup and all hyperparameters (8×H100, E5 retriever, 2018 Wikipedia corpus, default top-3, up to 4 search calls) | | C | Main results for the 14B model (average EM further improved to 0.479) | | D / E / F | Complete study on loss masking, base vs instruct, and PPO vs GRPO | | G | Retrieval top-k study (top-3 is optimal, 0.431) | | H | GRPO group size study (size=1 generalizes best, 0.410) | | I / J | Case comparison between R1 and Search-R1, plus more success and failure cases | The main text persuades, the appendix ensures reproducibility, and the boundaries are clean. The open-source repository includes complete datasets and checkpoints, and the 'reproducibility commitment' in the structure is fulfilled jointly by the appendix and the code. ## 6. Three Writing Techniques That Can Be Learned 1. **One figure explaining two algorithmic paths**: Figure 1 simultaneously depicts the rollout structures of PPO and GRPO, allowing readers to establish the understanding that 'this method is independent of specific RL algorithms' upon first encountering the framework, making the comparison in Section 5.1 less abrupt. 2. **Reward minimalism**: Pure EM rule-based rewards, with no format rewards and no process rewards, completely decoupling 'method effectiveness' from 'reward engineering complexity', making the conclusions more credible. 3. **Training dynamics plots as evidence**: The four-panel Figure 2 (algorithm comparison, base/instruct, length variation, search count) uses the same set of training curves to support four analytical conclusions, which is more persuasive than merely reporting final scores. ## Footnote: Mapping to My Own Work When building the post-match coaching system for QQ Speed, we established a separation of duties: the algorithm layer outputs structured evidence, while the LLM layer only performs semantic paraphrasing. Search-R1's loss masking is the version of this same idea on the training side: retrieval tokens belong to the environment, and policy gradients act only on tokens generated by the model itself. Information from the environment can enter the context, but the responsibility for updating weights must be clearly distinguished. In any training scenario where 'model-generated' and 'externally injected' content are mixed within a single sequence, this masking design is worth considering first. ## References - Paper: arXiv:2503.09516, published at COLM 2025 (The 2nd Conference on Language Modeling) - Code: github.com/PeterGriffinJin/Search-R1 - Main experimental scope: 7 datasets—NQ, TriviaQA, PopQA, HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, Musique, and Bamboogle. Among them, NQ and HotpotQA are in-domain, while the other five are out-of-domain. The metric used is Exact Match
